For decades, personalized financial guidance has been out of reach for most people. True wealth management required access to human advisors — costly, inconsistent, and often reserved for the top 1%. We made progress with the dawn of robo-advisors, but these still don’t go beyond static allocations and cookie-cutter recommendations. That gap is what Origin set out to close. Our AI Advisor brings human-level reasoning, continuous learning, and real-time adaptability to everyone — not just the ultra-wealthy. Every recommendation considers your actual data, market context, and long-term goals in real time. Here’s what that looks like in action:. Personalized answers at scale: The same depth of insight a CFP would offer, delivered instantly. Contextual reasoning: Guidance that adapts to new income, equity grants, or life changes as they happen. Continuous calibration: Models that learn and improve with every data point, interaction, and market event. This isn’t about convenience. It’s about changing who gets access to truly intelligent financial advice — aka what modern users now expect from an AI financial advisor. How Origin’s AI Advisor Works. Spending Agent: Analyzes trends, detects anomalies, and surfaces actionable cash flow insights. Planning Agent: Models long-term outcomes like retirement, tax scenarios, or liquidity events using Monte Carlo simulations. Compliance Layer: Validates every recommendation against fiduciary, privacy, and accuracy standards. These agents collaborate through a central orchestrator that routes every query to the right expert system. The result is end-to-end reasoning that mirrors a real advisory team, without the friction or cost. What Sets Origin’s AI Financial Advisor Apart. title: Law & AI – Latham Watkins Report – FCA Issues Guidance for Firms on Their Use of AI
excerpt: The guidance provides examples of good and poor practices and is designed to help firms apply the existing regulatory framework to their use of AI. Key POINTS:. The guidance focuses on three key areas: the Consumer Duty and vulnerable customers, governance and accountability, and operational resilience. An accompanying FCA speech confirms that the regulator is embedding the Mills Review’s recommendations into live work and that the FCA is itself becoming an “agentic regulator”. Supervisory scrutiny of firms’ AI use is set to increase, so firms should map their AI use cases against the good and poor practices using the action points we identify in this article, be ready to evidence how they meet the FCA’s expectations, and keep their approach under regular review. On 19 October 2026, the FCA published a webpage titled “AI in financial services: good practice and areas for improvement” which provides guidance for financial services firms using AI. While firms have welcomed the FCA’s pro-innovation stance and long-standing position that it will not introduce AI-specific regulation, they have found it challenging to understand how the existing regulatory framework should apply to the use of AI in new and untested scenarios. The FCA promised further guidance for firms following the publication of the House of Commons Treasury Select Committee report on AI in financial services at the start of the year. The report recommended that, by the end of 2026, the FCA should publish comprehensive, practical guidance for firms on: (a) the application of existing consumer protection rules (i. e. , the Consumer Duty) to their use of AI; and (b) accountability and the level of assurance expected from senior managers under the SMCR for harm caused through the use of AI (see this Latham blog post ). The publication of the guidance further cements the FCA’s position that it does not plan to introduce sector-specific rules on AI and will continue to rely on existing regulatory frameworks when supervising firms’ use of AI. With the FCA stating that 86% of firms are using AI, according to its latest biennial survey with the Bank of England on AI in UK financial services, the guidance is now more important than ever. The survey found that firms are using AI across a wider range of business areas and are increasingly reporting use of generative AI, AI-enabled agents, and third-party implementations of AI systems. In this article, we highlight key areas of the guidance and set out the most important action points for firms to consider to ensure that they are meeting regulatory expectations. To understand how the UK government and regulators’ positions on AI have developed over time, see our report “The AI Revolution: Navigating the Regulatory Landscape in UK Financial Services,” which draws together key publications and guidance to assist firms with understanding regulatory expectations. Good and Poor Practices. The FCA stresses that the examples it provides are relevant to a range of use cases and are designed to be illustrative only. It does not intend to create any new regulatory requirements or prescribe a particular approach in all cases. Consequently, firms should apply common sense and proportionality when mapping the guidance to their own use cases. The FCA also states that the guidance is not intended to be static; it will update the guidance as AI tools continue to develop. The good and poor practices cover three key areas, as detailed below. Consumer Duty and Vulnerable Customers. The key concern is that AI tools or solutions could result in consumer harm not adequately anticipated by the firm. The FCA explains that firms should design products and services to meet consumers’ needs, characteristics, and objectives, and explore whether AI can offer a solution, rather than being led by AI. title: Some Canadian banks blocking personal AI agents amid security concerns
excerpt: TORONTO — Some of Canada’s largest banks have moved to disallow third-party AI agents from accessing online banking. RBC spokesperson Jeff Lanthier confirmed the move in a statement Wednesday, saying the bank has decided to block third-party personal AI agents from direct access to authenticated RBC digital properties, including online banking. RBC CEO Dave McKay said in a post on LinkedIn on Tuesday evening that while the bank appreciates the benefits of AI being used to save time, “nothing is more important than the security of client information. ”. Stay up to top of Canada’s biggest banks with BNN Bloomberg’s Big Banks Tracker. “If AI is going to move beyond the frontier and into the broader economy, trust will matter as much as capability,” the post reads. BMO spokesperson John Fenton also said in a statement that it does not permit AI agents to access its digital properties or execute transactions in order to protect clients. TD Bank has said it made the decision to block third-party personal AI agents, while CIBC said it does not support personal AI agents directly opening or accessing accounts. National Bank said it is closely monitoring development of consumer AI agents. Scotiabank said it will limit third-party AI agents from its banking platforms while it monitors concerns. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026. Companies in this story: (TSX:BNS, TSX:NA, TSX:BMO, TSX:RY, TSX:TD, TSX:CM). Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press.

title: UBS and University of Oxford Launch Centre for Applied AI to Reshape Financial Services
excerpt: UBS has joined forces with the University of Oxford to launch the Oxford-UBS Centre for Applied Artificial Intelligence (AI), a strategic initiative designed to pioneer cutting-edge research and drive the practical application of AI within the financial services sector. The new Centre represents a ground-breaking interdisciplinary partnership involving UBS, Oxford Saïd Business School, and the University’s Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences (MPLS) division. Led by a newly endowed UBS Professor for Applied AI, the facility will be supported by a dedicated team of 20 researchers focusing on independent projects and joint initiatives where academic findings are tested against real-world banking scenarios. Bridging academia and application. The collaboration aims to move beyond theoretical models to produce practical tools that can be implemented at scale. The research mandate is split into three critical areas: AI and Society, covering governance, sustainability, and the Future of Work; AI for Business and Economy, examining innovation and ecosystem transformation; and AI Futures, which explores emerging paradigms and model developments. Mike Dargan , UBS group chief operations and technology officer, described the technology as a “fundamental opportunity” to change how the bank operates and creates value. “We are delighted that UBS will be partnering with the University of Oxford to foster pioneering AI research and develop practical tools and solutions that can be implemented at scale across our firm, accelerating our journey to become a fully AI-enabled institution and shaping the future of financial services,” Dargan said. Multidisciplinary approach. The partnership is distinct in its ability to draw intellectual capital from both Oxford’s business school and its scientific research division. Professor Irene Tracey , vice-chancellor of the University of Oxford, welcomed the collaboration as a union of a world-leading university and a top-tier financial institution. “This dynamic multidisciplinary partnership will lead to pioneering new AI research solutions and practical applications at a time of unprecedented technological change,” Tracey commented. “We are grateful to UBS for their vision and support, enabling us to launch the Oxford-UBS Centre for Applied AI. ”. As a leading wealth manager, UBS intends to harness the Centre’s output to deliver enhanced client solutions and increase employee productivity, positioning the bank at the forefront of the AI-driven shift in global finance. Switzerland has established itself as a leading hub for artificial intelligence (AI), ranking first in Europe in AI startup density in relation to population, and first in AI patents per one million inhabitants, according to Switzerland Global Enterprise, the country’s official organization for export and investment promotion. This burgeoning scene is further reflected by the growing volume of AI-related funding. In 2023, one in ten of all recorded funding rounds in Swiss startups was allocated to AI-related ventures, according to the EY Startup Barometer Switzerland 2025. This figure has doubled over the past year. In 2024, more than one in five funding rounds (22%) was invested in startups that operate in the AI field or use the new technology as an essential part of their offerings. Switzerland’s strength in AI is underpinned by the country’s world-renowned universities and research institutions in the field, including Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich (ETH Zurich), the Swiss Federal Technology Institute of Lausanne (EPFL), the University of St. Gallen, and the Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research (IDSIA) in Lugano. Top-tier research and talent have attracted the world’s tech giants, including Google , IBM , and Microsoft , which have all set up AI hubs in the country, further fueling Switzerland’s AI scene. Women have been at the forefront of this progress, driving AI innovation across academia, research, and the overall industry. They design strategies, write algorithms, and lead teams, helping shape the future of the field. To honor these leaders, the Greater Zurich Area, in collaboration with ETH AI Center at the ETH Zurich, released in September 2025 their top 100+ women in AI and data in Switzerland. Among these, eight women are standing out for their remarkable expertise and contributions to the finance sector, recognized for their leadership, vision, and ingenuity. Eleni Verteouri, Founder of Financier Labs, GenAI Tech Lead and Director at UBS. She also serves as generative AI (genAI) tech lead and director of conversational banking at UBS; a AI instructor at both ETH Zürich and ZHAW School of Management and Law; and a coach and mentor at Tenity, a fintech early-stage investor. A recognized leader in responsible AI, Verteouri has over a decade of impactful work in model development. She has made significant contributions to shaping modern fintech innovations as an acclaimed AI guest lecturer and advisor and a recipient of the Forbes Cyprus 20 Women in Tech Award 2024. She holds an MSc in quantitative finance from ETH Zurich and an MEng in electrical and computer engineering from the University of Patras. Dr. Sina Wulfmeyer, Chief Data Officer at Unique AI. Dr. Sina Wulfmeyer is the chief data officer at Unique AI, a European venture-backed business-to-business (B2B) software-as-a-service (SaaS) company pioneering advanced, responsible AI solutions for the financial services industry. At Unique, she oversees the development of FinanceGPT, an AI-driven platform designed to enhance customer relationships and increase productivity in the financial sector. With over 15 years of experience in AI and data strategy, Sina has held significant roles, including leading data-related projects at Credit Suisse and consulting at Accenture in Germany and the US. She is also an active lecturer and expert in fields such as General AI, Ecosystem Technology, and Data Protection, contributing to academia and industry conferences across Europe. title: NatWest cuts 1,000 jobs in three months as AI transformation accelerates
excerpt: Business & Support Services. Technology. Technology, Media & Telecoms. NatWest cuts 1,000 jobs in three months as AI transformation accelerates. Abm October 30, 2026. Share via:. Facebook. X. LinkedIn. WhatsApp. Pocket. Messenger. Telegram. NatWest Group (LON: NWG) has cut 1,000 jobs over the past three months as the banking giant accelerates its adoption of artificial intelligence, bringing total workforce reductions to 1,400 so far in 2026. The latest cuts mark a significant acceleration in the bank’s restructuring programme, with most of this year’s reductions taking place in the third quarter. Chief Executive Paul Thwaite confirmed that AI is reshaping roles across NatWest , creating new opportunities in technology while changing or reducing the need for some existing positions. The bank is increasingly using artificial intelligence to automate administrative processes, improve customer service and strengthen fraud detection. NatWest’s AI-powered customer service assistant, Cora, has handled 52,000 credit card-related customer issues , demonstrating the growing role of automated systems within its banking operations. Thwaite said the bank was creating positions specifically focused on artificial intelligence while adapting other roles to reflect changing technology requirements. He emphasised that NatWest’s objective was to ensure employees had the necessary skills to support the bank’s evolving operations. The workforce reductions come as major UK banks increasingly turn to AI to improve efficiency and reduce operating costs. Barclays recently outlined plans to cut approximately 5,000 jobs during 2026 , with artificial intelligence expected to play a significant role in reshaping its workforce. HSBC is also reportedly planning substantial reductions in its UK financial advisory operations as it introduces AI-driven services, while Standard Chartered has previously announced thousands of redundancies as part of its restructuring strategy. The developments highlight the growing impact of artificial intelligence on financial services employment, particularly in customer support, administration and other functions where technology can automate repetitive tasks. NatWest’s announcement coincided with third-quarter results showing a 3. 9% decline in profit to £1. 7 billion , partly reflecting a higher tax charge. Despite the year-on-year fall, the results were slightly ahead of City expectations , providing some reassurance about the bank’s underlying financial performance. The figures come shortly after the UK Government announced plans to increase taxation on banking profits in Chancellor John Healey’s Autumn Budget. The bank corporation tax surcharge will double from 3% to 6% for a temporary 15-month period beginning in January 2027 , increasing costs for major lenders. Thwaite stopped short of directly criticising the measure but stressed the importance of maintaining the proposed time limit. He argued that banks needed sufficient capital to support households and businesses, with a stable tax environment helping financial institutions plan investment and lending activities. The Chief Executive also reiterated NatWest’s ambition to expand its wealth management operations , reducing the group’s reliance on income sensitive to changes in interest rates. This strategy has been supported by the £2. 7 billion acquisition of Evelyn Partners , one of Britain’s largest wealth management businesses. The transaction represents NatWest’s largest acquisition since its involvement in the ABN Amro takeover before the global financial crisis. The latest reported workforce reductions exclude any employment changes associated with the Evelyn Partners acquisition. For investors, NatWest’s growing use of AI forms part of a wider effort to improve operational efficiency, strengthen customer services and diversify its revenue streams. However, the restructuring also raises questions about the longer-term impact of automation on employment within

From Swissquote to Reyl: Finance Veterans Back AI Startup. Backed by former banking heavyweights, Swiss startup Cigno has closed a 1. 5 million francs seed round to build out what it calls the AI infrastructure layer for management consulting. It is targeting financial services firms in Switzerland and Europe. The Leadership Team: Nicolas Lagrèze (COO),Philippe Reynier (CEO) and Vahan Avetisyan (CTO & Head of R&D). (Image: Courtesy). Monday, 18 May 2026 10:10. Written by: Florian Schwab | Publishing Director. Press play to listen to this content. 0:00. -:--. 1x. Playback Speed 0. 5. 0. 6. 0. 7. 0. 8. 0. 9. 1. 1. 1. 1. 2. 1. 3. 1. 5. 2. From Swissquote to Reyl: Finance Veterans Back AI Startup. Cigno was founded by Philippe Reynier (CEO), Nicolas Lagrèze (COO), and Vahan Avetisyan (CTO and Head of R&D). The Geneva-based startup automates the full consulting workflow, from research and data gathering through to structured recommendations, via multi-step workflows that replicate how consultants actually operate. The platform is built on a proprietary reasoning model and specialised agents. It targets a gap the founders see as systemic: generic large language models are not fit for professional consulting, given weak deliverable quality, unreliable data, no standardisation, and data sovereignty risks. Swiss Finance as Anchor Market. Cigno's first commercial wave has a clear sector focus. «Our first wave of consulting clients has a strong financial services practice in Switzerland and Europe,» Reynier told finews. «Their end clients are overwhelmingly Swiss and European banks, insurers and asset managers. Cigno is the AI infrastructure that enables these firms to deliver better and faster for their FS clients. ». The startup is incorporated as a Swiss entity with a sovereign-by-design architecture — European hosting, full client data isolation, and compliance infrastructure. Reynier describes this as «a prerequisite for Swiss financial institutions, and for the consultants who advise them. ». Former Bankers as Investors. The 1. 5 million seed round was closed exclusively with operators from consulting, finance and technology. Backers include Lino Finini, former Group COO of Swissquote, Pasha Bakhtiar, former Group CEO of Reyl Intesa Sanpaolo and co-founder of Alpian Bank, Niresh Rajah, former Group CDO of Danske Bank, Arnaud Denis, former Group CEO of MeDirect, Hazem Mulhim, founder and CEO of Eastnets, and former Credit Suisse executive Martin Mende. «I spent twenty years building the technological infrastructure that transformed Swissquote into a reference platform,» said Finini, who joins the board. «What I saw at Cigno is that same rigour: a team capable of building a real product in parallel with its fundraise. ». An Amplifier. Cigno's positioning is deliberately consultant-centric. Unlike tools that seek to disintermediate advisory firms, the platform enables each firm to encode its own methodology, sector expertise and client history into a structured, scalable asset — hosted in a controlled environment. Co-design workshops with around a hundred consulting leaders from major international firms informed the product architecture. Reynier draws an analogy with legal tech: «Entire verticals are realising that generic LLMs will never be enough, because the value does not lie in the model itself. It lies in data contextualisation, sovereignty, and the ability to encode a firm's proprietary methodology. ». Deployments From June 20

Künstliche Intelligenz: Nach KI-Investitionen: Großbank Barclays streicht 5.000 Jobs
excerpt: Die britische Großbank Barclays baut nach Investitionen in KI-Technologie 5000 Stellen ab. Foto: Yuki Iwamura/AP/dpa. London. Die britische Großbank Barclays will bis Ende des Jahres 5. 000 Stellen abbauen. Möglich wird das unter anderem durch den Einsatz von Künstlicher Intelligenz, wie das Unternehmen mitteilte. Ein Fünftel der Jobs sei bereits weggefallen, die übrigen 4. 000 sollten bis Ende des Jahres gestrichen werden. Der Stellenabbau ist demnach Teil größerer Sparmaßnahmen und entspreche etwa fünf Prozent der weltweit 93. 000 Beschäftigten. Der Großteil der Einsparungen betreffe das Privatkundengeschäft, teilweise aber auch das Investmentbanking. Abgebaut werden demnach überwiegend Stellen in internen Unterstützungs- und Zentralfunktionen. Dazu zähle auch der Abbau von Entwicklerstellen, da Künstliche Intelligenz die Produktivität erhöhe. Stellenabbau Ergebnis von Tech-Investitionen. Die Maßnahmen seien „das Ergebnis der Investitionen, die wir über mehrere Jahre hinweg in Technologie getätigt haben und weiterhin tätigen“, sagte Barclays-Chef C. S. Venkatakrishnan der britischen Nachrichtenagentur PA zufolge. „Wir werden KI in großem Umfang einsetzen. Aber KI ist das Sahnehäubchen auf der Torte, nicht die Torte selbst“, zitierte die „Financial Times“ den CEO. Bis Ende des Jahres will Barclays circa 300 Millionen Pfund (rund 358 Millionen Euro) einsparen. Damit geht ein dreijähriges Maßnahmenpaket zu Einsparungen und Investitionen in Technologie zu Ende. Für das dritte Quartal dieses Jahres verzeichnete die Großbank einen Vorsteuergewinn von 2,3 Milliarden Pfund (ca. 2,74 Milliarden Euro) - zwölf Prozent mehr als im Vorjahreszeitraum. title: The University of Oxford and UBS join forces to launch the Oxford-UBS Centre for Applied AI to pioneer research and innovation
excerpt: London / Zurich, December 9, 2025 – The University of Oxford and UBS are proud to announce the launch of the Oxford-UBS Centre for Applied Artificial Intelligence (AI). The Centre will aim to deepen the understanding of the power of AI through cutting-edge research and promote its practical application. The Centre aims to be a ground-breaking interdisciplinary partnership involving UBS, Oxford Saïd and the University’s Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences division (MPLS). It will drive independent research projects on AI as well as joint initiatives, in which Centre researchers collaborate closely with UBS practitioners to apply their findings to real-world applications. The Centre will be led by a newly endowed UBS Professor for Applied AI at Oxford Saïd and will be supported by a dedicated team of 20 researchers. Their research will focus on three key areas:. AI and Society : including aspects of AI governance, the Future of Work, and sustainability. AI for Business and Economy : including applications of AI in driving innovation and transformation across business and economic ecosystems. AI Futures : including the exploration of emerging AI paradigms, models developments and their applications. Welcoming news of the collaboration, Professor Irene Tracey, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford, said: “It is wonderful to announce this exciting and important partnership that brings together one of the world’s leading universities with a globally leading financial services institution. This dynamic multidisciplinary partnership will lead to pioneering new AI research solutions and practical applications at a time of unprecedented technological change. We are grateful to UBS for their vision and support, enabling us to launch the Oxford-UBS Centre for Applied AI. ”. Professor Tracey continued: “This strategic partnership will be unique in its research power as it draws on intellectual capital from the University of Oxford’s business school and our division for scientific research and is generously supported by UBS. ”. Mike Dargan, UBS Group Chief Operations and Technology Officer, said: “AI represents a fundamental opportunity to change how we operate and create value for clients. We are delighted that UBS will be partnering with the University of Oxford to foster pioneering AI research and develop practical tools and solutions that can be implemented at scale across our firm, accelerating our journey to become a fully AI-enabled institution and shaping the future of financial services. ” The Oxford-UBS Centre for Applied AI brings together two institutions with deep AI expertise and focus on innovation. The University of Oxford is a world leader in AI research, developing fundamental AI tools, using AI to tackle global challenges, and leading education and research in applied AI for business. As a leading wealth manager, UBS is harnessing the transformative capabilities of AI to deliver better client solutions and increase employee productivity. UBS Group AG. About UBS UBS is a leading and truly global wealth manager and the leading universal bank in Switzerland. It also provides diversified asset management solutions and focused investment banking capabilities. UBS manages 6. 9 trillion dollars of invested assets as per third quarter 2025. UBS helps clients achieve their financial goals through personalized advice, solutions and products. Headquartered in Zurich, Switzerland, the firm is operating in more than 50 markets around the globe. UBS Group shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). About the Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences (MPLS) Division The MPLS Division is home to the non-medical sciences at the University of Oxford. Its nine academic departments span the full spectrum of the mathematical, computational, physical, engineering and life sciences, carrying out world-leading research that ranges from fundamental discovery to cutting-edge applied work.
